evaluationApproach.summary: The AI must evaluate each response specifically for the Director of Coaching position. It must assess coaching philosophy, methodology, coach development, curriculum implementation, player-pathway alignment, quality assurance, collaboration, safeguarding and leadership judgment. There is no single required formation, curriculum brand, licensing system or coaching style.
evaluationApproach.corePrinciple: A strong response explains how coaching standards are defined, taught, observed, supported and improved across teams while preserving age-appropriate practice, coach ownership and player welfare.

mandatoryRules.rule: Score against Director of Coaching expectations, not Technical Director, Head Coach, Academy Director or general Club Administrator criteria.
Prioritize coach development, methodology implementation and coaching quality; do not require responsibility for all sporting strategy or recruitment.
Do not require one specific formation, curriculum, licensing pathway or coaching method; evaluate clarity, context and implementation.
For questions requesting a real situation, do not award 4/4 without the situation, action and outcome.
Reward age-appropriate alignment across teams; do not require identical tactics, sessions or coaching styles at every level.
Do not infer qualifications, safeguarding clearance, authority, impact or data literacy that the candidate did not demonstrate.
Flag contradictions between the written questionnaire and video response, but do not treat a contradiction alone as proof of dishonesty.
Do not reward humiliating, discriminatory, unsafe or punitive coaching practices, or promises of player and coach progression.
Do not score accent, grammar, appearance, age, gender, ethnicity, disability or production quality. Evaluate response content only.

humanReviewFlags: Ignoring, minimizing or concealing safeguarding, bullying, discriminatory conduct, injury or unsafe coaching practice.
Humiliating, threatening, coercive, discriminatory or developmentally inappropriate treatment of players or coaches.
Materially false or contradictory claims about qualifications, licenses, experience, authority or program impact.
Recruiting or retaining coaches without required identity, reference, safeguarding or background verification.
Evaluating coaches only through results, favoritism or one isolated observation while presenting the decision as objective.
Sharing confidential player, family, coach, medical, performance or employment information without authorization.
Using identical adult standards across youth age groups without regard to learning, maturation, welfare or context.
Routine micromanagement, public undermining of coaches or failure to act on persistent unsafe and non-compliant practice.

calibrationOverall.classification: Basic / acceptable; evidence or depth is limited
calibrationOverall.strongestAreas: Practical implementation of coaching standards; coherent training design; regular cross-functional communication
calibrationOverall.mainWeaknesses: Limited evidence of measurable outcomes, safeguarding procedures, age-group pathways, coach evaluation follow-up and implementation review
calibrationOverall.summary: The candidate demonstrates a basic understanding of the Director of Coaching role, with useful ideas for introducing shared coaching standards, designing purposeful sessions and collaborating with technical staff. However, the responses provide limited evidence of systematic coach evaluation, curriculum monitoring, safeguarding processes and measurable player-development outcomes. Further examples and supporting documentation would be needed to establish the depth and scale of the candidate's experience.

questions.text: Can you describe your professional background and pathway to becoming a Director of Coaching?
questions.evaluates: Relevant preparation, leadership progression and coaching-system experience.
strong: Identifies relevant coaching, education, licensing, mentoring, curriculum or club-leadership experience.
Explains progression from team delivery to responsibility for multiple coaches, teams or age groups.
Connects prior responsibilities to coach development, methodology and quality assurance.
Shows continuing learning and does not rely only on titles or years of service.
questions.acceptable: Describes relevant experience but gives limited detail about scale, responsibilities or progression.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Lists licenses or roles without explaining actual contribution, or presents team-coaching success as sufficient proof of club-wide leadership.

calibration.response: I coached youth teams for six years and later supported two new coaches with session planning.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Relevant coaching and mentoring experience; scope of director-level oversight is unclear.

questions.text: What is your coaching philosophy, and how has it evolved over time?
questions.evaluates: Philosophical clarity, evidence of learning and practical application.
strong: States clear beliefs about learning, player development, competition, relationships and coaching behavior.
Explains how the philosophy influences session design, feedback, playing opportunity and coach support.
Identifies specific experiences or evidence that changed earlier assumptions.
Allows contextual adaptation while preserving coherent principles.
questions.acceptable: Explains positive coaching beliefs and some evolution but gives limited practical application or evidence.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Uses generic slogans, copies a fashionable model, or cannot identify how beliefs affect coaching practice.

calibration.response: I believe players learn by making decisions. I now ask more questions than when I started.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: A clear philosophy and evolution, but limited concrete application.

questions.text: How do you define the role and responsibilities of a Director of Coaching within a club or organization?
strong: Defines responsibility for coaching standards, curriculum, coach recruitment, education, observation and support.
Explains oversight across teams and age groups with appropriate safeguarding and quality controls.
Distinguishes the role from Technical Director strategy and individual Head Coach match authority.
Recognizes reporting lines, resources, documentation and collaboration with club leadership.
questions.acceptable: Identifies coach management and methodology responsibilities but leaves governance or boundaries unclear.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Describes only coaching one team, claims unlimited technical authority or reduces the role to scheduling and administration.

calibration.response: I would help coaches use shared standards and observe their sessions.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Recognizes core responsibilities but omits governance and safeguarding processes.

questions.text: How do you evaluate tactical consistency across teams within the club?
questions.evaluates: Club-wide observation and age-appropriate tactical alignment.
strong: Defines observable principles by phase of play instead of requiring identical formations.
Uses training visits, match observation, plans, video and coach discussion across a planned cycle.
Allows age-, level- and context-appropriate variation while protecting shared principles.
Turns findings into coaching support, follow-up and documented improvement actions.
questions.acceptable: Describes observation and common principles but lacks indicators, cadence or age adaptation.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Equates consistency with one formation, judges through results alone or imposes first-team detail on all age groups.

calibration.response: I watch different teams and see whether they use our main principles.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Relevant approach, but no observation schedule or age-specific indicators.

questions.text: How do you ensure technical and tactical standards are implemented by coaches?
questions.evaluates: Standards communication, support and accountable follow-through.
strong: Translates standards into clear age-group outcomes, training behaviors and observable game principles.
Uses induction, curriculum resources, model sessions, mentoring and regular observation.
Provides specific feedback, improvement targets, resources and reasonable timelines.
Verifies implementation and distinguishes misunderstanding, resource limits and deliberate non-alignment.
questions.acceptable: Uses meetings, curriculum and observation but gives limited follow-up or support detail.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Issues standards without development support, evaluates only on wins or micromanages every coaching decision.

calibration.response: I introduce a curriculum, demonstrate sessions, then observe and give feedback to coaches.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Clear implementation process; follow-up measurement is not described.

questions.text: How do you analyze player and team performance data to guide coaching decisions?
questions.evaluates: Data literacy, contextual interpretation and coaching usefulness.
strong: Starts with a coaching or development question and selects relevant indicators.
Combines data with video, observation, role, age, maturation where relevant and competition context.
Checks data quality, sample size and limitations before drawing conclusions.
Converts findings into training priorities, player plans or coach reflection and reviews the effect.
questions.acceptable: Uses data and observation to inform coaching but gives limited validation, context or action.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Treats one metric as definitive, uses data to rank youth prematurely or confuses correlation with causation.

calibration.response: I look at match clips and basic statistics to see where teams struggle.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Uses relevant evidence, but does not address data quality, age context or actions.

questions.text: How do you design and implement a unified playing philosophy across all age groups?
questions.evaluates: Philosophy design, developmental progression and implementation.
strong: Defines observable principles in possession, defending, transitions and set plays.
Creates age-appropriate progressions rather than identical tactics or formations.
Connects the philosophy to curriculum, coach education, player profiles and assessment.
Pilots, communicates, observes and reviews implementation with stakeholder feedback.
questions.acceptable: Describes shared principles and age adaptation but gives limited implementation or review detail.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Copies another club, mandates identical tactics at every age or presents a document without an implementation process.

calibration.response: All teams should try to build from the back, with simpler expectations for younger players.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Shared principle and age adaptation, but incomplete club-wide implementation plan.

questions.text: What principles guide your coaching methodology in training and competition?
questions.evaluates: Coherent learning methodology and player-centered practice.
strong: Explains principles for objective-led design, realism, repetition, variability, feedback and player decision-making.
Balances development, challenge, enjoyment, welfare and competitive demands.
Adapts methods to age, ability, training age, context and session purpose.
Uses observation and reflection to adjust practice rather than following activities mechanically.
questions.acceptable: Names relevant training principles but provides limited connection to competition or adaptation.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Relies on drills without objectives, uses punitive coaching or treats one method as appropriate for every player and context.

calibration.response: Sessions should have one clear objective, realistic game situations and reflection afterward.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Coherent training principles with useful application, though evidence is limited.

questions.text: How do you ensure consistency while allowing coaches autonomy at different levels?
questions.evaluates: Leadership balance, minimum standards and professional trust.
strong: Defines non-negotiable principles, safeguarding expectations and required development outcomes.
Gives coaches autonomy over methods, session solutions and appropriate tactical detail.
Uses planning conversations, observation and reflective questions instead of constant prescription.
Intervenes proportionately when evidence shows risk, persistent non-alignment or support needs.
questions.acceptable: Recognizes shared standards and coach freedom but leaves boundaries or intervention criteria unclear.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Allows complete inconsistency, or controls every session and removes coach ownership and creativity.

calibration.response: Coaches can choose their exercises as long as they follow the club philosophy.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Appropriate autonomy, but boundaries and escalation are unspecified.

questions.text: How do you recruit, develop and evaluate coaches within the organization?
strong: Uses role profiles covering qualifications, behaviors, experience, availability and age-group fit.
Applies structured, fair selection with references and required safeguarding verification.
Provides induction, mentoring, observation, feedback and development objectives.
Uses periodic evaluation and transparent improvement or performance-management processes.
questions.acceptable: Describes recruitment, support and reviews but provides limited structure or fairness controls.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Recruits mainly through contacts, skips safeguarding checks, evaluates only results or removes coaches without documented support.

calibration.response: I recruit qualified coaches, watch their sessions and meet them to discuss improvement.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Relevant steps, but lacks fair selection, reference and safeguarding checks.

questions.text: What tools or indicators do you use to assess coaching performance?
questions.evaluates: Balanced coach evaluation and evidence quality.
strong: Uses planning quality, learning environment, communication, player engagement, session adaptation and standards implementation.
Combines observation, coach reflection, player-development evidence and appropriate feedback sources.
Uses agreed criteria, multiple observations and contextual interpretation.
Separates development feedback from formal performance decisions and records follow-up.
questions.acceptable: Uses observation and development indicators but lacks triangulation, consistency or follow-up.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Measures only wins, player popularity or personal style, or makes decisions from one visit or anonymous complaints alone.

calibration.response: I look at communication, organization and how much players participate.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Appropriate indicators; multiple observations and contextual review are missing.

questions.text: How do you support coaches in their professional development and licensing pathway?
questions.evaluates: Individualized development, mentoring and realistic progression support.
strong: Creates individual development plans based on role needs, observation, goals and career stage.
Uses mentoring, co-planning, model sessions, peer learning, resources and purposeful assignments.
Helps coaches understand licensing options and required experience without guaranteeing outcomes.
Reviews application of learning and adjusts support over time.
questions.acceptable: Offers courses, feedback and mentoring but gives limited individualization or transfer review.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Treats licensing as the only development measure, promises certification or provides training without follow-up.

calibration.response: I encourage licensing courses and share resources with the coaches.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Development support is present but not individualized or followed up.

questions.text: How do you align player-development objectives with long-term performance outcomes?
questions.evaluates: Pathway planning and balance between development and competition.
strong: Defines age- and stage-appropriate competencies linked to the club pathway and playing philosophy.
Uses individual plans, training objectives, playing opportunities and longitudinal review.
Balances current team contribution with longer-term learning and avoids early outcome bias.
Coordinates coaches and specialists while stating realistic uncertainty about future level.
questions.acceptable: Links development plans to pathway goals but gives limited review, opportunity or trade-off detail.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Prioritizes winning at all costs, promises progression or uses current physical dominance as the main potential measure.

calibration.response: I want each player to improve technically and eventually progress to higher teams.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Long-term aim, but no pathway measures or realistic transition criteria.

questions.text: How do you integrate physical, technical, tactical and mental development into a single framework?
strong: Defines interacting development outcomes rather than four disconnected departments.
Coordinates football training, individual work, physical development and age-appropriate behavioral support.
Uses shared plans, terminology, review points and clear specialist responsibilities.
Avoids unsupported psychological diagnosis and respects medical and professional scope.
questions.acceptable: Describes integrated planning and staff collaboration but gives limited ownership or practical sequencing.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Treats dimensions as isolated checklists, makes clinical claims or overloads players with uncoordinated programs.

calibration.response: I ask the physical coach and team coach to coordinate their plans.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Collaboration is useful but mental and tactical integration remains vague.

questions.text: How do you manage transitions between age groups and competitive levels?
questions.evaluates: Pathway continuity, readiness and transition support.
strong: Defines readiness through role-relevant behavior, development trajectory and next-level demands.
Uses shared player records, joint observations, handover meetings and planned exposure.
Coordinates communication with players, families and coaches appropriately.
Provides support, review and alternative pathways rather than treating promotion as a one-time judgment.
questions.acceptable: Uses assessments and staff handovers but gives limited transition support or review.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Promotes only by age or results, promises advancement, shares sensitive information casually or provides no support after movement.

calibration.response: We discuss players before moving them up and ask the next coach for feedback.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Some transition coordination; player support and readiness criteria are incomplete.

questions.text: How do you collaborate with Technical Directors, performance staff and management?
strong: Clarifies shared objectives, decision rights, meeting cadence and escalation routes.
Connects coaching delivery with technical strategy, player welfare, resources and organizational priorities.
Uses evidence and documented actions to resolve competing needs.
Protects coach responsibilities while seeking specialist input and maintaining confidentiality.
questions.acceptable: Describes regular collaboration and aligned planning but leaves decision rights or conflict resolution unclear.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Works in isolation, bypasses responsible staff or allows management pressure to replace player-centered coaching judgment.

calibration.response: I meet the Technical Director and performance staff monthly to align priorities and solve issues.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Concrete collaboration routine, but decision rights and escalation remain unclear.

questions.text: How do you measure the success of the coaching program at both individual and collective levels?
questions.evaluates: Balanced program evaluation and continuous improvement.
strong: Uses coach growth, curriculum implementation, learning environment, player progression, pathway movement and retention indicators.
Combines quantitative trends, observation, feedback and longitudinal evidence.
Recognizes that match results have multiple causes and avoids claiming direct causation.
Uses findings to improve staffing, education, curriculum and resource allocation.
questions.acceptable: Mentions coach and player development beyond results but gives limited measurement or review cadence.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Measures success only through league position, licenses obtained or satisfaction scores, or cannot connect evidence to improvement.

calibration.response: I check whether coaches improve and whether players enjoy sessions and develop.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Balanced indicators but no measurement cadence or evidence sources.

questions.text: If you were appointed today, what would be your priorities in the first 90 days?
questions.evaluates: Diagnostic planning, prioritization and change leadership.
strong: Begins with listening, safeguarding and compliance checks, role clarification and observation of current practice.
Maps coaches, teams, curriculum, resources, player pathway and urgent risks before major change.
Defines a small number of priorities, owners, timelines and communication routines.
Delivers early support while producing an evidence-based longer-term plan and review point.
questions.acceptable: Proposes assessment, meetings and initial priorities but gives limited sequencing, ownership or risk attention.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Immediately replaces systems or coaches without diagnosis, promises rapid transformation or focuses on branding before player and coach needs.

calibration.response: I would meet the staff, observe training, and identify three priorities for the next season.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Reasonable initial diagnosis but misses urgent safeguarding review and 90-day ownership.
